lines.text: It translates Hindi perfectly — but can't write your mum's birthday card.
Reading and writing look like one skill. Inside the machine, they are two.
Reading and writing are the same thing. If it understands my sentence, it can write one.
Bet. If understanding were enough, your translator could write your mum's birthday card. Lunch says it can't.
One paper, in 2017, put them in one box — 'Attention Is All You Need'. Attention is how the model weighs which words matter most. Look inside.
Think of a team translating a book. First, someone reads the whole chapter.
Then someone else writes it in the new language, one word at a time — checking the original after every word.
Models that translate or summarise often use both halves. But GPT uses only the decoder.
A writer that reads its own writing as it goes.
GPT never reads the way you think. It only writes — and reading its own writing is the whole trick.
Then show me the two halves doing two jobs.
Same sentence. Two machines.
The decoder writes the birthday message, word by word. The encoder sorts the documents — sorting is reading and understanding what each one says.
An agent does the next thing — write the reply, call the tool, take the next step. A tool is another program it can use.
But if GPT only writes, how does it understand my question at all?
It doesn't understand the way you do — your question goes in first, as the starting input. Then it predicts the next word — again and again.
The transformer reads, then writes. GPT keeps only the writer.
Not a movie robot. A writer robot. And I owe you lunch.
Next episode — how is such a model actually built? In two stages, and the order matters. Get it backwards and you waste millions.
Encoder or decoder — which half would your job need more, reading or writing? Tell us.
